title: How the Liza act was built and hiding Fats from alimony collectors
summary: The female singer was the glamour of such acts while the band was his; Fats had to be hidden on arrival in towns because of unpaid alimony.

bands.name: Edith Wilson and her Jazz Hounds

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Now tell me about Liza, all this is so interesting, I want to pull out some of these things. Liza was like -- what was she -- a singer, right?
She was a singer, Katie Crippen. She was our singer, blues singer, and we hired --
She was the leader, she -- this was her band.
No, it wasn't her band, no, no, no. We called it as an act, Liza and her Shuffling Sextet.

But we had hired her to sing, but you have to have a feature attraction in a vaudeville act. You have a center. The act was built around her, you see, and -- as a singer, and she did a little dance and she was the glamour of the act, you see. Five big rough men in tuxedos and all, but she was the glamour, nice looking girl. So you had an act like that you always -- the woman singer, you say, so and so and her jazzband. Mamie Smith and her Jazz -- Edith Wilson and her Jazz Hounds --
I see, but the band was like -- the band itself --

It was my band, my group. And Fats Waller, God bless him -- we used to have so much fun with him. Fats would come to the theater -- he always bought apples on a stick, you know, then he would get around 270, 285 pounds. He'd come down the street, wabbling down the street with one of these apples on a stick and every time we'd have to go we'd have to hide him because the law was always after him for non-payment of alimony, you know.
Oh, yes, she was -- every town we hit, "Fats?" No, he's not here -- we'd have to hide him first couple days. Sometimes we'd have to hire a pianist to play the first day.
